performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: A stern phrase for brass and strings, answered by one violin over a harp: the Sultan and Scheherazade are already in the room. Pierre Monteux conducts the San Francisco Symphony, with Naoum Blinder as the storyteller.

sections.label: Intro · Brass and strings in unison
sections.mNote: The Sultan’s descending phrase, marked Largo e maestoso

sections.label: Frame · Violin over harp chords
sections.mNote: The violin’s winding recitative introduces Scheherazade

sections.label: A · Strings set the waves moving
sections.mNote: Allegro non troppo: rolling accompaniment beneath the long tune

sections.label: B · Solo winds between the waves
sections.mNote: Horn and woodwind solos replace the massed orchestra

sections.label: Dev · Strings and brass gather again
sections.mNote: The sea tune grows above the moving strings

sections.mNote: The broad tune rides over the rolling accompaniment

sections.label: Coda · The waves settle in E major

cues.title: The Sultan’s first word
cues.text: Brass, low woodwinds and strings deliver a descending phrase in octaves. Largo e maestoso — broad and majestic. The strings press heavily into their notes, and pauses break up the phrase before the winds answer softly.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, pp. 1–2: Largo e maestoso, strings marked pesante, and the quiet wind chords. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One violin answers
cues.text: Scheherazade’s violin winds above the harp. The score marks it Recitativo: a singer’s freedom, with no words. After the orchestra’s heavy opening, Naoum Blinder has room to turn a single phrase into a tale.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, p. 2: Lento, Recitativo, solo violin and harp. Blinder is credited in the recording documentation: https://archive.org/metadata/Sheherazade/metadata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The strings make waves
cues.text: Allegro non troppo. The strings begin their rolling accompaniment, and the Sultan’s stern phrase becomes the broad sea tune. Its long notes ride over the quicker motion below; the same melody has put out to sea.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, p. 2 onwards. Paul Serotsky describes the opening motto’s transformation into the sea music: https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three years at sea
cues.text: At twelve, Rimsky-Korsakov enters naval college. He begins his First Symphony before a three-year voyage, then returns to a life divided between music and the navy. For years his jobs include inspecting naval bands.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, LA Philharmonic programme note, documents the naval training, voyage, First Symphony and band-inspection work. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade-last-movement

cues.title: A story buys another night
cues.text: In The Thousand and One Nights, Scheherazade keeps her husband waiting for the end of each story. The Sultan postpones her execution to hear what happens next. Rimsky-Korsakov gives this woman one violin against a whole orchestra.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass, LA Philharmonic programme note, explains the framing tale and the solo violin’s association with Scheherazade. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade

cues.title: San Francisco, March 1942
cues.text: Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony make this recording at the War Memorial Opera House on 3–4 March 1942. Naoum Blinder plays the violin solos. The complete suite fills Victor’s 78-rpm album DM-920.
cues.evidence: The original transfer documentation gives the venue, sessions, performers and Victor album number. https://archive.org/metadata/Sheherazade/metadata

cues.title: The sea tune returns
cues.text: The broad sea tune returns over the rolling strings. Brass and strings enlarge a melody that began as the Sultan’s solitary command. The accompaniment keeps rising and falling beneath its long notes.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, later return of the Allegro material; Serotsky describes the alternating orchestral crests and quieter solo episodes. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E major, at rest
cues.text: The closing pages settle into E major. Small solo phrases remain among the strings and winds; at the very end a cello’s rising and falling figure rests beneath held wind chords. The strings finish with soft plucked notes.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement, closing pages, especially p. 23: solo cello, sustained winds and pizzicato strings. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Wind chords leave room for violin
transitions.from: Intro · Brass and strings in unison
transitions.how: The heavy opening stops. Soft wind chords, separated by fermatas, prepare the violin’s Lento recitative. Harp chords replace the orchestral bass, and the violin climbs into its winding, espressivo line.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement, pp. 1–2, from the opening wind chords to Lento, Recitativo. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf

transitions.title: The strings begin to roll
transitions.to: A · Strings set the waves moving
transitions.how: A cadenza and held violin note end the recitative. At Allegro non troppo, the key signature changes to E minor. Violas and cellos begin their rolling figures; the violins take up the broad tune above them, with winds sustaining the harmony.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement, p. 2, the end of the violin cadenza and opening Allegro non troppo. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/a2f9ec91cec0e2d1d7dd842aa83ea8fb.pdf

source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, I, full-score scan
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–2: the opening phrase, wind chords and violin recitative; pp. 10 and 18: piccolo, brass and timpani with the sea tune; pp. 21–23: closing wind chords, solo cello and plucked strings.

timeline.note: Low winds, brass and strings state the heavy opening phrase in octaves.
Quiet woodwind chords answer the opening phrase, with pauses between them.
The solo violin begins its recitative above harp chords.
At Allegro non troppo, moving violas and cellos carry the waves beneath the violin tune.
Piccolo, brass and timpani join the winds and strings as the sea tune grows.
Woodwind solos emerge between the strings’ rolling phrases.
High winds, brass and timpani reinforce the strings’ rolling accompaniment.
Wind solos and string replies emerge as the brass falls silent.
The sea tune returns with the strings, winds and brass.
Held wind chords settle above the strings’ continuing motion.
A solo cello winds beneath held woodwinds; plucked string chords finish the E-major cadence.

composer.epithet: He became a professor before he could write counterpoint, then built Russian fairy-tale operas around an orchestra he knew instrument by instrument.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856; piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 for a voyage lasting nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, snatching a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev and received encouragement with requests for changes. Farther out, he watched the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue and saw flying fish and phosphorescence. Back in Russia, music reclaimed him; Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
